newsitem.title: INDIA: India's caution masks unease over Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: India's caution masks unease over Afghanistan.

text.p: The Taleban militia's sudden victories in Afghanistan have set off alarm bells in India, where the rise of Islamic fundamentalism is perceived as a potential menace to Kashmir and Delhi's ties to Central Asia.
Publicly, India reacted cautiously to the Taleban's weekend gains. "The situation is entirely within the domestic sphere of Afghanistan," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement on Monday.
The guarded response contrasted with stinging criticism of the Taleban last year before the militia had consolidated their hold over most of Afghanistan.

In November, Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, who was then foreign minister, called the Taleban obscurantist, accused them of denying women's rights and pledged support to ousted president Burhanuddin Rabbani.

India's new-found caution reflects the ground reality in Afghanistan, where the Taleban swept northward at the weekend, tightening their grip over the country after support for opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum collapsed.
Dostum, who fled to Turkey, and Rabbani had been bound in a fragile coalition that now stands in tatters -- and with it, India's policy of backing the ousted president.
"This is a major setback for India," the Asian Age newspaper said in an editorial.

India's prudence masked deep unease over the impact the Taleban's brand of Islamic fundamentalism could have on a separatist insurgency in Kashmir and New Delhi's drive to strengthen ties with Central Asia, diplomats and analysts said.
"It is a bad thing for India," said J.N. Dixit, former Indian ambassador to Kabul.
Indian policymakers were concerned Taleban militia might eventually turn their sights towards Kashmir once they tightened their grip over Afghanistan.
Mostly Hindu India is fighting a revolt by Moslem separatists in the Himalayan region, where more than 20,000 people have died in insurgency-related violence since 1990.

India accuses Pakistan of arming and training guerrillas fighting New Delhi's rule in Kashmir. India's Islamic neighbour, which rules over one-third of Kashmir, says it provides only moral and diplomatic backing.
New Delhi has also accused Pakistan of aiding Taleban warriors. Islamabad says it is neutral.
"There is some speculation that Kashmir will worsen because of this," said B.G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research, an independent think-tank in New Delhi.

"The Taleban have not succeeded without Pakistani and Saudi support and U.S. endorsement," said Dixit, formerly India's top career diplomat. "The U.S. might not be happy, but if Pakistan wants to divert militant cadres to Kashmir, they will do so."
India was also concerned that an unfriendly regime in Kabul, allied with Islamabad, could smother its efforts to gain access to Central Asia's oil and natural gas reserves.
"In the short term, a hostile Afghanistan affects access to Central Asia," Dixit said.

"We were hoping to get, in due course, oil and natural gas from Turkmenistan. If we establish good terms with the Taleban, yes, but in the initial stages, they will not be very happy about it," he said.

Analysts said Delhi would stick to its wait-and-see stance until the Taleban demonstrated they were free from outside control, unwilling to support Islamic militancy in Central Asia and able to reconcile Afghanistan's numerous ethnic groups.
"The situation is very fluid," said an analyst who asked not to be identified. "There is no pressure on India to take any action right now."

But analysts said India would eventually have to abandon its support for Rabbani and recognise the Taleban, provided the Islamic militia consolidated their grip over the country. "It's only a matter of time," Verghese said.
